item.title: Your parcel is having a random day
item.author: sarbhanu.baidya+work@gmail.com (Sarbhanu Baidya)
item.description:
You order something online. The app says your package has left the warehouse. A few hours later, it reaches your city. The next morning, you get a notification: Out for delivery. And then… nothing.

You check the app again. Still out for delivery. An hour passes. Same notification. You begin wondering whether the delivery person is stuck in traffic, having lunch, looking for your address or perhaps delivering twenty other packages before yours. It is an ordinary experience, but here is an interesting thought: can we describe the journey of that package using mathematics? Not by drawing its geographical route or calculating the distance between two locations. Instead, imagine describing what the package is doing at any given moment and how likely it is to change what it is doing next.

This is where the theory probability meets everyday life.

A package doesn’t just travel. It changes states.

Think about the possible situations your package can be in. It might be waiting at a warehouse, assigned to a delivery agent, travelling through the city or delayed by traffic. Eventually, it gets delivered. Or perhaps the customer isn’t home and the entire process has to be repeated. Let’s forget about the geographical route for a moment. Suppose we care only about the current state of the package. We can represent its journey as:

$$ W\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow T\longrightarrow D $$

where $W$ represents the warehouse, $A$ the assigned state, $T$ the in-transit state and $D$ the delivered state. The package occupies one state at a time and moves between states at random instants. We do not know exactly when the next transition will occur. However, we can describe the probabilities governing these transitions. To understand how, let’s begin with something familiar.

The Poisson Process: Counting random events

Suppose our package is waiting at the warehouse to be assigned to a delivery agent. How long will it wait? Perhaps five minutes, perhaps forty. There is no fixed schedule that guarantees when the assignment will happen. Imagine that assignment opportunities occur randomly at a constant average rate of $0.8$ per hour. This is precisely the kind of situation we can describe using a Poisson Process.

Let $N(t)$ denote the number of assignment opportunities occurring during a period of $t$ hours. Then:

$$ N(t)\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(0.8t) $$

The probability of observing exactly $n$ assignment opportunities is:

$$ P(N(t)=n)=\frac{e^{-0.8t}(0.8t)^n}{n!} $$

Now, what is the probability that no assignment opportunity occurs during the next hour? Putting $t=1$ and $n=0$, we obtain:

$$ \begin{aligned} P(N(1)=0) &=\frac{e^{-0.8}(0.8)^0}{0!}\\ &=e^{-0.8}\\ &\approx0.4493 \end{aligned} $$

Thus, there is approximately a $44.93\%$ probability that no assignment opportunity occurs during the next hour. Consequently, the probability of at least one opportunity is:

$$ P(N(1)\geq1)=1-e^{-0.8}\approx0.5507 $$

In other words, there is approximately a $55.07\%$ probability of at least one assignment opportunity within an hour. But there is another interesting connection. The waiting time until the first event of a Poisson Process follows an exponential distribution. If $T$ denotes the waiting time until the first assignment opportunity, then: $P(T>t)=e^{-0.8t}$

This connection is important because exponentially distributed holding times are fundamental to Continuous Time Markov Chains (CTMC).

From Poisson Processes to CTMC

A Poisson Process counts random events occurring over time. A Continuous-Time Markov Chain describes how a system changes its state as these events occur.

Let’s extend our delivery example. Suppose the transition rates between the states are:

Transition Rate per hour
Warehouse to Assigned 0.8
Assigned to In transit 1.2
In transit to Delivered 0.5

These rates are hypothetical and are chosen simply to illustrate the mathematics.

Since the waiting time in each state follows an exponential distribution, the expected time spent in each state is the reciprocal of its transition rate. Thus:

$$ \begin{aligned} E[T_W]&=\frac{1}{0.8}=1.25,\\ E[T_A]&=\frac{1}{1.2}\approx0.8333,\\ E[T_T]&=\frac{1}{0.5}=2. \end{aligned} $$

Since the package must pass through all three stages, its expected delivery time is:

$$ \begin{aligned} E[T_D] &=1.25+0.8333+2\\ &\approx4.0833\text{ hours}. \end{aligned} $$

So, under our simplified model, the expected time from the warehouse to successful delivery is approximately 4.08 hours. Of course, an expected value does not tell us where the package is likely to be at a particular instant. For that, we need to describe the transitions collectively.

The Generator Matrix: The DNA of a CTMC

The generator matrix, usually denoted by $G$, contains the instantaneous transition rates of the entire Markov chain. To understand its structure, suppose we have a CTMC with states $S_1,S_2,\ldots,S_n$. Its generator matrix is:

$$ G= \begin{bmatrix} g_{11}&g_{12}&\cdots&g_{1n}\\ g_{21}&g_{22}&\cdots&g_{2n}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ g_{n1}&g_{n2}&\cdots&g_{nn} \end{bmatrix} $$

For distinct states $i$ and $j$, the off-diagonal entry $g_{ij}$ represents the transition rate from state $i$ to state $j$:

$$ g_{ij}=\lim_{h\to0^+} \frac{P(X(t+h)=j\mid X(t)=i)}{h}, \qquad i\neq j. $$

The diagonal entries are determined by the condition that every row sums to zero, i.e. $g_{ii}=-\sum_{j\neq i}g_{ij}$

Consequently, the generator matrix has three important properties:

  1. Every off-diagonal entry is non-negative.
  2. Every diagonal entry is non-positive.
  3. Every row sums to zero.

For our delivery model, the only possible transitions are $W\to A$, $A\to T$ and $T\to D$. Therefore, the generator matrix becomes:

$$ G= \left[ \begin{array}{c|cccc} & W & A & T & D\\ \hline W & -0.8 & 0.8 & 0 & 0\\ A & 0 & -1.2 & 1.2 & 0\\ T & 0 & 0 & -0.5 & 0.5\\ D & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] $$

The off-diagonal entries represent the transition rates from one state to another, while the diagonal entries represent the negative total rate of leaving each state. For example, $g_{12}=0.8$ represents the rate at which a package moves from the warehouse to the assigned state. Similarly, $g_{23}=1.2$ represents the rate of moving from assigned to in transit.

Why is the first diagonal entry $-0.8$? Because the only possible way to leave the warehouse is to enter the assigned state. Hence, $g_{11}=-0.8$. The same reasoning applies to the other transient states. Notice that the final row consists entirely of zeros. We have assumed that the delivered state is absorbing, meaning that once a package reaches this state, it remains there. The generator matrix provides a compact mathematical description of the entire delivery process.

More formally, for a small time interval $\Delta h$:

$$ P(X(t+h)=j\mid X(t)=i) =g_{ij}h+o(h),\quad i\neq j $$

while:

$$ P(X(t+h)=i\mid X(t)=i) =1+g_{ii}h+o(h). $$

Here, $o(h)$ represents terms that become negligible compared with $h$ as $h$ approaches zero. In simple terms, the generator matrix describes the instantaneous behaviour of the system.

Where is the package likely to be after two hours?

Let $P(t)$ denote the transition probability matrix. Its individual entries are defined by:

$$ p_{ij}(t)=P(X(t)=j\mid X(0)=i) $$

This tells us the probability that a package starting in state $i$ will be in state $j$ after $t$ hours.

For a time-homogeneous CTMC, the transition probability matrix is given by: $P(t)=e^{Gt}$. The matrix exponential connects instantaneous transition rates to probabilities over an entire period of time.

Suppose our package starts at the warehouse. Its initial probability distribution is:

$$ p(0)= \begin{bmatrix} 1&0&0&0 \end{bmatrix} $$

After two hours:

$$ p(2)=p(0)e^{2G} $$

Evaluating the matrix exponential gives approximately:

$$ p(2)= \begin{bmatrix} 0.2019&0.2224&0.3776&0.1982 \end{bmatrix} $$

The entries correspond to the following probabilities:

Package state Probability after 2 hours
At warehouse 20.19%
Assigned to courier 22.24%
In transit 37.76%
Delivered 19.82%

Think about that for a moment. Even though the package started at the warehouse, there is approximately a $19.82\%$ probability that it has already been delivered after two hours. At the same time, there is still approximately a $20.19\%$ probability that it hasn’t even left the warehouse!

This is the advantage of modelling the process probabilistically. Rather than predicting one particular outcome, we obtain a distribution over all possible states.

The Kolmogorov Forward Equation: Watching probabilities flow

We have calculated the probabilities at a particular instant. But what if we want to understand how these probabilities change continuously? This brings us to the Kolmogorov forward equation:

$$ \frac{dP(t)}{dt}=P(t)G $$

If $p(t)$ represents the probability distribution as a row vector, then:

$$ \frac{dp(t)}{dt}=p(t)G $$

Substituting our generator matrix gives:

$$ \begin{aligned} p_W'(t)&=-0.8p_W(t),\\ p_A'(t)&=0.8p_W(t)-1.2p_A(t),\\ p_T'(t)&=1.2p_A(t)-0.5p_T(t),\\ p_D'(t)&=0.5p_T(t). \end{aligned} $$

Consider the third equation:

$$ p_T'(t)=1.2p_A(t)-0.5p_T(t) $$

The probability of being in transit increases as packages enter from the assigned state. At the same time, it decreases as packages leave the transit state and get delivered. Thus, the rate of change is simply the probability flowing in minus the probability flowing out. This is essentially a balance equation for probabilities. We are watching probability flow through a delivery system, much like packages flow through a logistics network.

The Kolmogorov Backward Equation: Looking from the beginning

Now let’s approach the same problem from a different perspective. Suppose if we ask: if a package starts at the warehouse, what is the probability that it will be delivered within the next two hours?

Define:

$$ h_i(t)=P(X(t)=D\mid X(0)=i) $$

Here, $h_i(t)$ represents the probability of being in the delivered state after time $t$, given that the package started in state $i$.

The Kolmogorov backward equation is:

$$ \frac{dP(t)}{dt}=GP(t) $$

For our delivery probability vector, written as a column vector $h(t)$, it becomes:

$$ \frac{dh(t)}{dt}=Gh(t) $$

Our system of equations is therefore:

$$ \begin{aligned} h_W'(t)&=0.8[h_A(t)-h_W(t)],\\ h_A'(t)&=1.2[h_T(t)-h_A(t)],\\ h_T'(t)&=0.5[h_D(t)-h_T(t)],\\ h_D'(t)&=0. \end{aligned} $$

The initial conditions are:

$$ h_W(0)=h_A(0)=h_T(0)=0,\qquad h_D(0)=1. $$

The reasoning is simple. If the package starts at the warehouse, in the assigned state or in transit, it has not yet been delivered at time zero. If it starts in the delivered state, the delivery is already complete.

Solving this system gives:

$$ \begin{aligned} h_W(t)=1 &-\frac{32}{7}e^{-0.5t}\\ &+5e^{-0.8t}\\ &-\frac{10}{7}e^{-1.2t}. \end{aligned} $$

Now substitute $t=2$:

$$ \begin{aligned} h_W(2) ={}&1-\frac{32}{7}e^{-1}\\ &+5e^{-1.6}\\ &-\frac{10}{7}e^{-2.4}\\ \approx{}&0.1982. \end{aligned} $$

Therefore, there is approximately a $19.82\%$ probability that a package starting at the warehouse will be in the delivered state after two hours. This is exactly the probability we obtained from the delivered state entry of the transition probability matrix, from another perspective.

The forward equation describes how the probability distribution evolves from an initial distribution. The backward equation describes how the probability of a future outcome depends on the starting state. Both offer different ways of looking at the same stochastic system.

What if we make the delivery system more realistic?

Our four-state model is deliberately simple. Real deliveries rarely follow such a neat progression. A package might encounter traffic congestion, an unsuccessful delivery attempt, an unavailable customer or a return to the distribution centre.

We could introduce additional states, for example:

$$ T\longrightarrow C\longrightarrow T $$

where $C$ represents traffic congestion. Similarly:

$$ T\longrightarrow F\longrightarrow R $$

where $F$ represents a failed delivery attempt and $R$ represents a return to the warehouse. Each additional state introduces new transition rates and changes the generator matrix.

We could even move beyond an individual package and model an entire delivery fleet. The state might represent the number of available couriers, the number of occupied couriers or the number of packages awaiting assignment. There is one modelling consideration worth remembering. Standard CTMCs assume exponentially distributed holding times and constant transition rates. Actual delivery durations may follow other distributions and traffic conditions may vary throughout the day. More realistic models might therefore require time dependent transition rates or semi-Markov processes.

But the simple model gives us a starting point.

Final thoughts

There is something I like about this particular application of CTMCs. We usually encounter stochastic processes through abstract states, transition matrices and differential equations. It is easy to forget that these mathematical objects can describe the unpredictability of ordinary life.

A delivery notification is just a small piece of information displayed on a phone. Behind it is a sequence of events that nobody can predict perfectly. A package waits. Someone picks it up. Traffic slows it down. A customer misses the delivery. Another attempt is made. A Poisson Process helps us describe the random occurrence of events. The generator matrix captures the rates at which the system changes. The Kolmogorov equations describe how probabilities evolve.

And suddenly, an ordinary parcel journey becomes a continuous time stochastic process. Perhaps the next time your parcel gets stuck at Out for delivery, you’ll see more than an annoying notification. You’ll see a little probability theory unfolding in real time.

item.title: $1000, a slot machine and 5 choices
item.author: sarbhanu.baidya+work@gmail.com (Sarbhanu Baidya)
item.description:
Imagine you’re in Vegas with $1000 in hand. In front of you is a slot machine. Every time you play, you can choose one of five options:

$$ [S1\ |\ S2\ |\ S3\ |\ S4\ |\ S5] $$

You don’t know which option is better or worse. You don’t know their individual probabilities or payout distributions. All you know is that if you randomly choose one of the five options for a $1 play, the expected payout is $$x$. So, how should you use your $1000?

You could divide it equally among the five options. You could spend some of it testing the options and then put the remaining money on whichever one looks best, or you could continue experimenting throughout the game.

This looks like a standard exploration-exploitation problem, but there is a more fundamental statistical question that comes first: is the information we have enough to determine an optimal strategy?

The Game

Let the true expected payout of option $i$ be $\mu_i$, where $i\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}$. Suppose the only thing we know about these expected payouts is their average:

$$ \frac{\mu_1+\mu_2+\mu_3+\mu_4+\mu_5}{5}=x $$

For example, let $x=0.95$. The five expected payouts could be:

$$ (0.94,0.95,0.96,0.95,0.95) $$

or they could be:

$$ (0.60,0.70,0.90,1.00,1.55) $$

Both satisfy the same constraint, but the value of exploration is very different in the two cases. If the five options are nearly identical, spending a large part of the bankroll trying to identify the best one is unlikely to be useful. If one option is substantially better than the others, identifying it early could have a large effect on the final bankroll.

The problem is that we don’t know which situation we’re in.

The Problem With Picking the Winner

Suppose we play each option 10 times and obtain:

Option Played Returned Observed return
1 $10 $8 80%
2 $10 $11 110%
3 $10 $9 90%
4 $10 $7 70%
5 $10 $18 180%

Option 5 looks like the winner, but 10 observations are not enough to know whether its underlying expected payout is actually higher or whether we have simply observed a favorable sequence of outcomes.

We therefore have two competing uses for the remaining bankroll. We can exploit the information we have and play the option that currently looks best, or we can spend some of the bankroll collecting additional information.

A simple approach would be to choose an exploration budget in advance. For example, we could spend $20 on each option, for a total of $100, and then use the remaining $900 on the option with the highest observed return. We could compare this with other fixed budgets:

Exploration budget Exploration per option Remaining bankroll
$50 $10 $950
$100 $20 $900
$150 $30 $850
$200 $40 $800
$300 $60 $700

Monte Carlo simulation could compare the average final bankroll produced by these strategies. But this immediately raises another question: why should the exploration budget be fixed in advance?

If the evidence after $40 strongly favors one option, continuing to explore may be wasteful. If the evidence is still ambiguous after $200, stopping simply because the predetermined budget has been exhausted may also be wasteful.

Ideally, the decision to explore should depend on the information accumulated so far.

What Can We Infer From the Data?

After each $1 play, we observe another payout. We can use these observations to update our estimates of the five expected payouts. Suppose that at some point our estimates are:

$$ \mu_1\approx0.91,\quad \mu_2\approx0.94,\quad \mu_3\approx0.96,\quad \mu_4\approx1.03,\quad \mu_5\approx0.93 $$

Option 4 currently has the highest estimated return, but the estimates alone do not tell us how uncertain they are. An estimate of $1.03$ based on three observations is very different from an estimate of $1.03$ based on 300 observations.

This is where a probabilistic model becomes useful. Rather than treating each $\mu_i$ as a single estimated number, we can represent our uncertainty about it with a probability distribution.

In a Bayesian formulation, if $D_t$ denotes the observations collected after $t$ plays, we work with a posterior distribution such as:

$$ P(\mu_i\mid D_t) $$

This allows us to quantify statements such as the probability that a particular option is actually the best. For example:

$$ P(\text{Option 4 is best}\mid D_t)=0.97 $$

would mean that, under our model and prior assumptions, there is a 97% posterior probability that option 4 has the highest expected payout.

But even a high probability of having identified the best option does not automatically tell us to stop exploring. The difference between the options also matters. If option 4 is probably best but is expected to be only marginally better than option 3, another observation might still be useful. If option 4 appears to be dramatically better, further exploration may have very little value. This brings us to the value of information.

Exploration as a Decision Problem

Suppose there are $600 left in the bankroll. We could use the next $1 on the option that currently looks best, or we could use it to gather more information about another option.

The second choice has an immediate cost: we give up the opportunity to exploit our current information with that $1. But the resulting observation could change what we do with the remaining $599.

The relevant quantity is therefore not simply the expected payout of the exploratory play. It is the expected improvement in future decisions caused by the information that play provides.

Conceptually, we want to compare the expected final bankroll from exploiting now with the expected final bankroll from collecting another observation and then making better decisions with the information it provides.

If the latter is larger, exploration is worthwhile. If it is smaller, exploitation is preferable.

This is a sequential decision problem because the decision at time $t$ depends on the information collected before time $t$ and on how much of the bankroll remains.

The policy can be written as:

$$ \pi(H_t)\rightarrow\{1,2,3,4,5\} $$

where $H_t$ represents the complete history of observations up to play $t$. The objective is: $\max_{\pi}E_\pi[B_{\text{final}}]$, where $B_{\text{final}}$ is the final bankroll.

But There Is a Fundamental Problem

There is an important limitation that is easy to overlook. The equation:

$$ \frac{\mu_1+\mu_2+\mu_3+\mu_4+\mu_5}{5}=x $$

does not define a probability distribution over the unknown $\mu_i$. It only defines a constraint.

There are infinitely many possible combinations of expected payouts that satisfy it. We therefore cannot simply run a Monte Carlo simulation and claim that it tells us the optimal strategy. To simulate the unknown state of the machine, we need to specify how likely the different possible states are.

This requires an additional modeling assumption. For example, we could specify a prior distribution over the five expected payouts, subject to their average being $x$:

$$ P(\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3,\mu_4,\mu_5\mid x) $$

The prior represents our uncertainty before observing any plays. It might assign most of its probability to situations where the five options are similar, or it might allow substantial differences between them.

This assumption is not contained in the original problem. We are adding it in order to make the decision problem well-defined.

That distinction is important because changing the prior can change the optimal strategy.

Monte Carlo Comes After the Model

Once we have specified a model for the unknown machine, Monte Carlo gives us a practical way to evaluate a strategy. A single simulation run still contains only one player and one $1000 bankroll. We first generate a possible hidden state of the five options from the model. The player does not observe that hidden state. The player only sees the outcomes of the plays they choose to make.

The strategy then uses the available information to decide where to spend each $1. After every observation, it updates its beliefs and chooses the next action.

When the $1000 has been exhausted, we record the final bankroll. We then repeat the entire experiment many times. Each run represents a different possible realization of the same decision problem. For example:

Run 1 → $1137
Run 2 → $812
Run 3 → $1264
Run 4 → $947

After enough repetitions, the average final bankroll estimates:

$$ E[B_{\text{final}}\mid\text{strategy, model}] $$

We can then compare different policies under the same model. For example, we could compare random selection, a greedy strategy that always chooses the current estimated winner, several fixed exploration budgets and an adaptive policy based on the posterior distribution.

The purpose of Monte Carlo here is not to discover the unknown $\mu_i$ directly. It is to evaluate the consequences of different decision rules under an explicitly specified model of uncertainty.

The Prior Changes the Value of Exploration

This gives us a useful experiment in its own right. Suppose one prior says that the five options are almost always similar. Under that prior, extensive exploration is unlikely to produce much useful information, so a strategy that exploits relatively early may perform well.

Now consider a different prior that allows one option to be substantially better than the others. In that setting, exploration becomes more valuable because identifying the best option can affect a large portion of the remaining bankroll.

The two models can therefore produce different optimal policies even though they have the same overall expected payout $x$. This means there is no universal answer such as “spend 10% of the bankroll exploring.” The amount of exploration depends on what we assume about the uncertainty in the underlying choices.

Information About One Option Can Affect the Others

There is also an interesting consequence of the constraint on the expected payouts. Suppose we know:

$$ \mu_1+\mu_2+\mu_3+\mu_4+\mu_5=5x $$

and $x=0.95$, so that:

$$ \mu_1+\mu_2+\mu_3+\mu_4+\mu_5=4.75 $$

If we somehow knew:

$$ \mu_1=0.80,\quad \mu_2=0.85,\quad \mu_3=0.90,\quad \mu_4=1.00 $$

then the fifth expected payout would have to be:

$$ \mu_5=4.75-(0.80+0.85+0.90+1.00)=1.20 $$

In practice, our estimates would have uncertainty, so we would not normally know $\mu_5$ exactly. But information about the first four options would still provide information about the fifth because the five expected payouts are linked by the constraint. This means that the choices are not necessarily independent from an inference perspective. Learning about one part of the system can change what we believe about another part.

What We Can Actually Answer

The original question sounds simple:

How much of the $1000 should I spend figuring out which option is best?

But the answer cannot be obtained from $x$ alone.

The first thing we need is a probability model describing our uncertainty about the unknown options. Once that model is specified, we can update it after every play and use the resulting posterior distribution to evaluate the expected value of further information.

The decision then becomes a sequential optimization problem:

$$ \max_{\pi}E_\pi[B_{\text{final}}] $$

where the policy $\pi$ decides where to spend each $1 based on everything observed so far. Monte Carlo can then be used to compare those policies and estimate their expected final bankrolls. So the interesting question is not really whether $100, $200 or $300 is the “correct” exploration budget. There may not be a fixed exploration budget at all.

The more fundamental question is:

Given a particular model of uncertainty about the five choices, how should a $1000 bankroll be allocated between learning and exploiting what has already been learned?

That is a problem we can actually simulate, analyze and test.

item.title: Correlation vs. causation?
item.author: sarbhanu.baidya+work@gmail.com (Sarbhanu Baidya)
item.description:
View on LinkedIn

Ever noticed how sometimes two things move in sync, but one doesn’t necessarily cause the other? Here’s why we should dig deeper:

Key Considerations:

  • Confounding Variables: Other hidden factors might be at play.
  • Reverse Causality: What if the effect is actually causing the cause?
  • Coincidental Correlation: Some patterns are just happy coincidences.

Two classic examples from Statistics 101:

  1. Ice cream sales & Shark attacks: Correlation: Positive, but in reality: Seasonal effects come into play (people swim more in Summer and eat more ice cream)
  2. Height & Reading Ability in Children: Correlation: Positive, but actually: Age is the key (Of course, older kids are taller and better readers)

Digging Past the Usual: To truly understand causation, we need to go beyond mere observation and utilize techniques like randomized controlled trials, natural experiments, or instrumental variables.

Simpson’s Paradox: Sometimes, a trend that appears in different groups of data disappears or reverses when these groups are combined. Always analyze data within the right context.

Pearl’s do-operator: p(y|do(x)) ≠ p(y|x). This concept from Judea Pearl helps distinguish between mere correlation and causation by simulating an intervention in the model.

Always Ask: “What’s the underlying mechanism?”

Stay curious and keep questioning!

#CausalInference #DataScience
